newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serb hardliners ignore Plavsic demonstrations.
newsitem.headline: Serb hardliners ignore Plavsic demonstrations.

text.p: A conflict in the Bosnian Serb republic between President Biljana Plavsic and hardliners threatening to derail peace efforts will be raised at the NATO summit in Madrid, U.S. envoy Robert Gelbard said on Saturday.

He offered support to Plavsic at a meeting in Banja Luka in north Bosnia before leaving for Sunday's summit and told reporters: "These problems will be on the agenda. They must be solved at once in keeping with the law and Dayton (the Bosnian peace agreement."
But nationalists loyal to ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic kept up their pressure on Plavsic to end the dispute on their terms.
They ordered her to return from Banja Luka to their government seat in Pale to face parliament or be dismissed.

During Bosnia's 43-month-long war, Plavsic had a reputation no less hardline towards her mainly Moslem foes than Karadzic himself, but since the Dayton peace accord she has adopted a pragmatic line in an effort to gain foreign aid and investment.
Gelbard made clear that international lawyers were satisfied Plavsic acted within the constitution when she disbanded the parliament this week and called elections for September 1.
He said threats against NATO peacekeepers by Karadzic's police would be punished and added: "I do not want to go into details but it will be serious."
Mediators implementing the peace agreement said they would take no notice of the parliament meeting attended only by members of Karadzic's ruling SDS parliament.

"The assembly which is just now taking place is a private meeting of members of a totalitarian party and its allies," Michael Steiner, deputy to the international High Representative to Bosnia, told reporters.
"Whatever they decide -- it will have no legal effect."

Plavsic, a loyal deputy to Karadzic during the 1992-95 war pitting Serb separatists against pro-independence governmment forces, has called for an end to rampant corruption and urged cooperation with international peacemakers.

International envoys feared that two parallel governments could emerge, one in Banja Luka and the other in Pale, or that her replacement by a hard-line nominee would damage the already troubled Bosnian peace process.

Members of the ruling SDS party, covertly controlled by war-time leader Karadzic, called on Plavsic to resign at the second day of the session on Saturday held at a ski resort near their stronghold of Pale, outside Sarajevo.

Government officials, who portrayed Plavsic as a pawn of Western powers, said they were confident they would prevail because they controlled a large police force, the media and had obtained the support of neighbouring Yugoslavia.
They said Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic had pledged to support the hardliners and expected him to deliver the votes of Socialist deputies needed to launch recall proceedings against Plavsic.
Senior officials of the ruling SDS party brushed aside her allegations that corruption involving Karadzic and state-owned companies in the Bosnian Serb republic was being protected by the police.
They claimed she violated her constitutional rights by trying dissolve parliament and suspend police chief Dragan Kijac, an important Karadzic loyalist.

Plavsic embarked on her conflict with the hardliners a week ago when she tried to suspend Kijac for refusing to investigate two suspect state companies involving Karadzic and his senior aide Momcilo Krajisnik.
Defending himself in parliament, Kijac claimed Plavsic was the victim of foreign manipulation intended to harm the Bosnian Serb republic by driving a wedge between her and the SDS leadership.
The hardliners were moving to isolate Plavsic as they had others in the past who tried to take on Karadzic, including former Bosnian Serb Prime Minister Rajko Kasagic.
Western envoys last year promoted Kasagic as more a pragmatic alternative to Karadzic but he was removed and labelled a traitor by the hardliners in Pale.
